newsitem.title: JORDAN: King Hussein sacks PM Kabariti for veteran Majali.
newsitem.headline: King Hussein sacks PM Kabariti for veteran Majali.

text.p: King Hussein of Jordan has dismissed Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti and replaced him with a veteran former premier who signed Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel, officials said on Wednesday.
Kabariti told reporters after a special cabinet session on Wednesday he was offering his resignation to the king, who had picked 71-year-old Abdul-Salam al-Majali to form the new government.
Kabariti gave no reason for his sudden removal, but he suggested it was connected to a recent flare-up of tensions with Israel.
"Events and the changes, either locally or regionally, always take us by surprise and this is Jordan's fate to be always in the centre of events and storms," he said.
The official Petra news agency said Majali had already begun consultations to appoint his new ministers.

"His Majesty wanted to have a new start and he wanted to choose Abdul-Salam al-Majali to lead the new team for the coming period so as to continue with the path of reform and reconstruction and give some more vigour to our role, whether in the Arab role or in the region," Kabariti said before heading for the royal palace.
A Jordanian soldier shot dead seven Israeli schoolgirls last week after Jordan warned Israel that its plans to build a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem could provoke violence.
King Hussein visited the site of the attack and consoled the Israeli families of the victims in Jerusalem but Kabariti, who was also defence and foreign minister, stayed away both times.
Some observers said Kabariti was unhappy at the king's decision to meet Netanyahu in Jerusalem, just one week after he rebuked him for pushing the Middle East "towards the abyss of bloodshed."
Majali, who as prime minister from 1993 to 1995 also oversaw Jordan's first multi-party elections for decades, was picking a new cabinet to lead Jordan into scheduled November elections.
A cabinet reshuffle had been widely expected before the elections but the king's decision to replace Kabariti surprised some observers.

Ten days ago the monarch called on Kabariti, appointed in February last year with a mandate for sweeping economic and administrative reform which became known as the "white revolution", to step up the pace of change.

"I said to him if he still had the same enthusiasm, honesty, bravery, integrity and righteousness which we know he has...we will look at future issues with a new style," the king was quoted as saying. "But if he is scared of confronting storms... we will have to think of another solution."

Kabariti's government, backed by the International Monetary Fund, pushed through controversial cuts in bread price subsidies which led to rioting last August. It had also tabled legislation to reform company laws, customs and the Amman stock exchange.
The king's replacement of Kabariti, 47, with Majali marks not only a return to an earlier generation of premiers, but a different style of leadership.
"Majali is more of a delegator, their styles are completely different," said one analyst, adding he expected Majali to head a caretaker government to see Jordan through the elections.

Two cabinet ministers announced their resignation from Kabariti's government in the last four months, citing Kabariti's "overbearing" style of leadership and his restricting of decision-making to an inner circle of ministers. One subsequently withdrew his resignation.
"Majali is an old politician who has been around for many years," commented one former minister. "He signed the peace treaty with Israel and supervised the previous elections."
"His appointment is an indication of focussing on the peace again," he added.
He said Jordan also had good relations with Iraq during Majali's period in office. King Hussein subsequently turned against President Saddam Hussein and Kabariti was seen as spearheading that move.

Since Iraq signed a deal with the United Nations allowing it to export oil worth $2 billion every six months to buy food and medicines, Jordan's business community has been campaigning for better ties with Baghdad to help them secure contracts.
